Modern.brandNameRationale: Bookmatching is the woodworking technique of slicing a board in two and opening it like a book so the two halves mirror each other across a seam. The technique is a documented term in the trade. & Co. closes it as a small modern shop.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern woodworking has split between mass-import cabinetry and a small considered-modern cohort of independent shops. The opening is for a studio that puts the grain technique itself in the brand position and builds a small permanent catalog from the bookmatched panel.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Sawkille Co. (sawkille.com) holds the considered-modern American woodworking position. Atelier de Troupe (atelierdetroupe.com) sits in the design-led wood-and-craft tier. Egg Collective (eggcollective.com) is the studio-furniture peer. We sit closer to Sawkille in posture with a sharper bookmatched-panel specialty.
Modern.positioningStatement: A modern woodworking studio whose tables and casework are organized around the bookmatched panel.

targetAudience.primary: 32 to 55. Owns one home and is furnishing it slowly. Can name the wood when shown the grain. Buys one piece every two years and keeps it.
behaviors: Researches the species before the order
Will wait nine months for the right slab

dos: Show the grain match on the page
Name the wood and the joiner
Quote the panel dimensions in inches
donts: Photograph the piece in styled lofts

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark — Bookmatch & Co. set in a clean modern grotesk, with a small two-leaf bookmatched-grain mark beside the word. The mark alone serves as the brand on the underside of every top.

typography.primary: Söhne for the wordmark and headlines
typography.secondary: Söhne for body and product cards
typography.rationale: One family across the system. The brand is the grain, not the type.

Luxury.tagline: The butterfly joint, since the slab.
Luxury.brandNameRationale: The butterfly (or 'bow-tie') joint is the wood inlay laid across a crack to stop it from spreading — a documented Japanese and American Studio-Craft technique most associated with George Nakashima's slab tables, but the joint itself is a public-domain craft term. Atelier closes it as a small bench-craft house.
Luxury.industrySummary: Luxury woodworking at the slab-and-bench tier has been dominated by a few estate-protected names. The opening underneath is for a small atelier built on the joint itself rather than any single maker's surname — a house that takes a limited number of commissioned tables a year and signs them by joint count.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: BDDW (bddw.com) holds the American studio-craft luxury slot. Wexler Gallery (wexlergallery.com) is the design-edition gallery peer. Mira Nakashima Studio (nakashimawoodworkers.com) is the canonical reference — we sit beside it, not in its shadow, with a sharper joint-as-brand framing.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A small commission atelier for tables organized around the butterfly joint.

targetAudience.primary: 55 to 80. Multi-generational collector. Owns at least one Studio-Craft piece. Commissions a single table a year for a specific room.
behaviors: Travels to the workshop for the slab selection
Pays in three installments over eighteen months

dos: Show the joint, not the slab
Speak in the language of figure and check
Sign each piece by joint count

Luxury.logoDirection: A serif wordmark — Butterfly Joint Atelier set in a classical roman, with a small embossed bow-tie joint as the hallmark. The hallmark is branded on the underside of every commissioned top and embossed on the certificate of provenance.

typography.primary: Canela for the wordmark and certificates
typography.secondary: Adobe Garamond for body and commission documents
typography.rationale: Canela carries the Studio-Craft display tradition. Garamond keeps the documentation warm.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: A tenon is the projecting tongue cut on the end of one piece of wood, designed to fit into a mortise in another — the foundational hand-cut joint of Western and Eastern joinery alike. Single trade word, single syllable, terminal period. The brand is the joint.
Minimal.industrySummary: Minimal woodworking has converged on Scandinavian visual cues. The opening underneath is the joint itself — a different vocabulary of restraint, organized around the cut rather than the surface finish.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Skagerak (skagerak.dk) holds the Scandinavian-modern peer slot. Frama (framacph.com) sits in the considered-Nordic tier. De La Espada (delaespada.com) is the considered-craft peer. We sit closer to De La Espada with a single-joint focus.
Minimal.positioningStatement: Minimal furniture organized around the mortise-and-tenon joint.

targetAudience.primary: 30 to 55. Owns a small home. Studies joinery in books. Will wait six months for the right piece.
behaviors: Studies the joint, not the surface
Buys one piece every three years

dos: Name the wood and the joiner
donts: Use the word minimal as marketing
Photograph the piece in styled rooms

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark only — Tenon. set in a calm humanist sans, lowercase, terminal period. The favicon is the period.

typography.primary: Neue Haas Grotesk for the wordmark and body
typography.rationale: One face. The brand is the joint, not the type.

Corporate.tagline: Cabinetry and joinery for the architectural specification.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Heartwood is the dense, durable inner core of a tree — the timber grade specified in architectural millwork for load-bearing and finished work. Joinery is the trade name. Co. closes it as a serious commercial millwork firm.
Corporate.industrySummary: Architectural millwork is a serious B2B category. The buyers are architects, GCs, and FF&E consultants. The vendors compete on shop drawings, lead time, and on-site fit across thousands of feet of casework.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Bulthaup (bulthaup.com) is the institutional architectural-cabinetry benchmark. Henrybuilt (henrybuilt.com) holds the considered-American peer slot. Christian Liaigre's Métropolitain millwork tier sets the European reference. We sit smaller, more responsive on the spec sheet.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Architectural millwork and joinery for the spec sheet — durable, drawn, on schedule.

targetAudience.primary: 45 to 60. Architects, project architects, and FF&E consultants. Manage multi-million-dollar fit-outs.
behaviors: Requests shop drawings and 3D models first

dos: Quote lead times to the week

Corporate.logoDirection: A wordmark with a small geometric mark — a stylized cross-section of a tree showing heartwood at the core. HEARTWOOD JOINERY CO. set in a tight modern grotesk, suitable for spec books, name badges, and trade-show banners.

typography.primary: Inter for marketing and B2B materials
typography.secondary: Source Serif Pro for printed shop drawings and RFPs
typography.rationale: Inter scales clean across digital. The serif handles printed AWI documentation.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Steam-bending is the technique of softening a wood blank in steam so it can be clamped around a former and dried into a curve — the foundational technique of the Windsor chair, the bentwood Thonet, and Sam Maloof's rockers. The Goat is the absurd noun pairing; the brand is a steam-bent workshop with a sense of humor.
Creative.industrySummary: Creative woodworking has been crowded with maximalist live-edge slabs. The opening is for a studio working in the steam-bent tradition — Windsor, Thonet, Maloof — with a small permanent catalog of chairs and rockers, signed and dated.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Hierve (hierve.com) holds the conceptual-craft slot. Studio Henry Wilson (henrywilson.com.au) sits in the design-edition tier. Fyrn (fyrn.com) plays the considered-stickback chair peer. We sit beside Fyrn with a sharper steam-bend specialty.
Creative.positioningStatement: A witty, steam-bent woodworking studio in the Windsor-Thonet-Maloof tradition.

targetAudience.primary: 30 to 50. Design-literate buyer. Owns at least one Windsor or Thonet. Reads about furniture history. Buys for the chair, not the room.

dos: Show the chair in a working kitchen

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark — The Steam-Bent Goat set in a punchy display sans with a small drawn mark of a goat standing on a curved chair-leg. The goat alone is the favicon.

typography.primary: PP Mori for the wordmark and headlines
typography.secondary: GT Sectra for product descriptions and editorial
typography.rationale: Mori carries the wit. Sectra makes the workshop notes feel like a small craft journal.
